title: OLED
description: Diode that emits light from an organic compound
wiki_lead:
An organic light-emitting diode (OLED), also known as organic electroluminescent (organic EL) diode, is a type of light-emitting diode (LED) in which the emissive electroluminescent layer is an organic compound film that emits light in response to an electric current. This organic layer is situated between two electrodes; typically, at least one of these electrodes is transparent. OLEDs are used to create digital displays in devices such as television screens, computer monitors, and portable systems such as smartphones and handheld game consoles; its significant advantage over liquid-crystal displays (LCD) is that the individual pixels emit their own light, requiring no backlight like LED-lit LCDs. 
OLEDs are fundamentally different from LEDs and do not employ a crystalline structure. There are two main families of OLED: those based on small molecules and those employing polymers. Adding mobile ions to an OLED creates a light-emitting electrochemical cell (LEC) which has a slightly different mode of operation. An OLED display matrix can have various control schemes:

A passive-matrix (PMOLED) where each row and line in the display is controlled sequentially, one by one
Active-matrix (AMOLED) that uses a thin-film transistor (TFT) backplane to directly access and switch each individual pixel on or off, allowing for higher resolution and larger display sizes.
The invention of OLED can be attributed to two chemists at Eastman Kodak in 1987, namely Ching Wan Tang and Steven Van Slyke. Its public commercial use began with a car stereo in 1997 by Pioneer and for more than a decade its use was mainly for small monochrome displays in-car or portable systems, although the first full-color OLED display was implemented in a Kodak digicam in 2003. OLED displays took off during the latter half of the 2010s and have since been implemented mainly in wearable devices, smartphones, and high-end televisions.

History

André Bernanose and co-workers at the Nancy-Université made the first observations of electroluminescence in organic materials, in the early 1950s. They applied high alternating voltages in air to materials such as acridine orange dye, either deposited on or dissolved in cellulose or cellophane thin films. The proposed mechanism was either direct excitation of the dye molecules or excitation of electrons.
In 1960, Martin Pope and co-workers at New York University developed ohmic dark-injecting electrode contacts to organic crystals. They further described the necessary energetic requirements (work functions) for hole and electron injecting electrode contacts. These contacts are the basis of charge injection in all modern OLED devices. Pope's group also first observed direct current (DC) electroluminescence under vacuum on a single pure crystal of anthracene and on anthracene crystals doped with tetracene in 1963 using a small area silver electrode at 400 volts. grok_lead: Organic Light-Emitting Diode (OLED) is a thin-film electroluminescent technology that utilizes organic semiconductor materials to produce light when an electric current passes through them, enabling self-emissive displays and lighting solutions without the need for a backlight. This process relies on the recombination of electrons and holes in the organic layers to generate photons, offering superior image quality with perfect blacks, infinite contrast ratios, and neutral, highly accurate colors due to pixel-level light control that allows individual pixels to be turned off completely, surpassing those of LCD-based displays including LED and Mini-LED backlit models which rely on local dimming zones that can cause blooming and halo effects. OLEDs have become a cornerstone of modern consumer electronics, powering high-resolution screens in smartphones, televisions, and wearables due to their flexibility and energy efficiency. In online communities such as Reddit discussions and Brazilian forums, OLED TVs are frequently recommended by film enthusiasts for their effective brightness reduction (reduÃ§Ã£o de brilho), providing perfect blacks through complete pixel shutoff in dark areas, neutral and accurate colors, and superior contrast compared to LED/Mini-LED TVs, with particular praise for dark room viewing and suitability for cinematic experiences owing to good low-level performance and less aggressive peak brightness in many scenarios. The fundamental structure of an OLED consists of multiple thin organic layersâtypically including a hole-injection layer, hole-transport layer, emissive layer, electron-transport layer, and electron-injection layerâsandwiched between an anode (often indium tin oxide) and a cathode (such as calcium or aluminum). When voltage is applied, positive charges (holes) move from the anode and negative charges (electrons) from the cathode into the emissive layer, where they recombine to form excitons that decay radiatively, emitting light whose color depends on the organic material's bandgap. Efficiency is enhanced through mechanisms like phosphorescence or thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF), with external quantum efficiencies (EQE) reaching up to over 40% in recent advanced designs (as of 2025). Key advantages of OLED technology include its ultra-thin profile (often under 1 mm), lightweight construction, and potential for flexible or curved forms, making it ideal for innovative applications like foldable devices and wearable displays. It provides wide viewing angles exceeding 160 degrees, response times under 1 microsecond, and high brightness exceeding 5,000 cd/mÂ² in laboratory devices, while consuming less power than LCDs for similar luminance levels. In lighting, OLEDs offer tunable white light with a color rendering index (CRI) near 100 and mercury-free operation, contributing to energy savings in general illumination. OLEDs were pioneered in the late 1980s, with the first practical low-voltage device demonstrated in 1987 by Ching W. Tang and Steven Van Slyke at Eastman Kodak, marking a breakthrough in organic electroluminescence. Commercial adoption accelerated in the 2000s for small displays, evolving to large-panel televisions by the 2010s, and in 2025, the global OLED panel revenue reached approximately $53 billion, slightly down from $54 billion in 2024 amid intense competition. While Chinese manufacturers (including BOE, Visionox, and Tianma) increased their combined shipment share to over 50% (from 47% in 2024), Korean firms Samsung Display and LG Display maintained leadership in premium and high-value segments, with Samsung Display holding 48% of revenue share and LG Display 21%. Despite challenges like material degradationâparticularly for blue emitters, where lifetimes remain shorter (e.g., LT50 exceeding 800 hours at 1000 cd/mÂ² for advanced TADF devices)âongoing research in TADF and phosphorescent materials continues to improve stability and efficiency. Applications extend beyond consumer electronics to automotive lighting, medical sensors, and architectural panels, underscoring OLED's versatility in advancing display and illumination technologies.
